interviewQuestions.question: What makes a postmortem "blameless," and why does it matter?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Blameless means the investigation's questions target the **system** — why did our tooling, process, or safeguards let this happen — rather than the **person** who happened to trigger it. It doesn't mean nobody made a mistake, and it doesn't mean no accountability; action items still get real owners and due dates.

Why it matters practically: if engineers expect to be blamed, they give vague or defensive answers, or quietly omit the detail that actually explains the failure — "I missed the review comment because I was context-switching between three things" becomes a sanitized "the review process could be clearer." That missing detail is exactly what a good fix needs, so a blame-focused process systematically produces worse postmortems, not just meaner ones.

I've seen the difference firsthand: a blameless culture gets people volunteering "I actually wasn't sure what that config did, and nothing flagged it," which points straight at a real fix — better documentation or a validation check. A blame-focused version of the same incident gets a much thinner account and a much weaker fix.

**Testing:** whether you understand blameless as a mechanism for better information, not just a nicer tone.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through how you'd use the 5 whys on a real incident, and where the technique can go wrong.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from the observed failure and ask why, repeatedly, treating each answer as the next thing to interrogate rather than a stopping point. A concrete example: checkout failed → the payment service crashed → it ran out of memory → a cache grew unbounded → there was no eviction policy configured → the cache library defaults to unbounded and nothing in review or CI catches that.

Stopping early — at "it ran out of memory," say — leads to a fix like "give it more memory," which addresses this specific instance and leaves the actual defect, an unconfigured eviction policy with no safety net catching it, fully intact for the next service that makes the same omission. Reaching the fifth why gets to something systemic and actionable: a CI check for unbounded cache configuration protects every future service, not just this one.

Where the technique goes wrong: treating five as a magic number rather than "deep enough to reach something systemic" — sometimes that's three whys, sometimes it's seven. It can also derail into a single linear chain when the real cause is several contributing factors that each needed a why of their own; I'd rather run a short why-chain per contributing factor than force everything into one line.

**Testing:** whether you can apply the technique with judgment rather than mechanically counting to five.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Root cause analysis

interviewQuestions.question: A postmortem concludes the incident happened because "an engineer pushed a bad config." How would you push the analysis further?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd treat that as the trigger, not the cause, and ask what else had to be true for that trigger to become a customer-facing incident. A bad config on its own doesn't cause an outage — it has to also pass review unnoticed, deploy without a canary or staged rollout catching it, and reach a system with no circuit breaker or validation to contain the blast radius. Four things had to align, and the postmortem as written only addresses one.

Concretely I'd push the team to list every contributing factor they can identify and propose an action item for more than just the trigger: could a canary stage have caught this regardless of what the bad change was? Could a config-validation step in CI have rejected it structurally? Could an alert have fired on the specific metric sooner, cutting detection time?

The reason this matters beyond thoroughness: fixing only the trigger ("remind engineers to be careful with configs") doesn't survive the next engineer's equally human mistake, which is guaranteed to happen eventually to someone. Fixing the systemic gaps — canary, validation, circuit breaker — protects against triggers nobody has thought of yet, which is the actual goal of a postmortem.

**Testing:** whether you push past a single, convenient root cause toward the full stack of contributing factors, which is the senior-level version of postmortem analysis.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Systems thinking

interviewQuestions.question: Your team writes thorough postmortems, but you've noticed the same category of incident keeps recurring. What would you investigate?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My first hypothesis wouldn't be that the analysis is weak — thorough postmortems with recurring incidents almost always points at the **action items**, not the write-ups. I'd pull the last several postmortems for this category and check, concretely, what fraction of their action items actually got completed, and how long the completed ones took.

The pattern I'd expect to find: action items assigned to a team rather than a named owner, no due date, or tracked only inside the postmortem document rather than as a real ticket in the normal backlog — all three make an action item invisible to normal prioritization, so it quietly loses to whatever feature work is more urgent that sprint. Writing sharp analysis feels like the finish line, but the analysis itself prevents nothing; only the follow-through does.

What I'd push for: every action item gets a named individual owner and a due date at postmortem time, entered as a ticket in the team's actual work tracker immediately (not "we'll file it later"), and a recurring, separate review of open postmortem action items — treating an old unresolved high-value item as a signal worth escalating on its own, the same way a live incident would be.

If even that doesn't close the gap, I'd look one level higher: maybe the postmortems keep identifying the same *type* of systemic gap (say, always "no canary stage") across different incidents, which would suggest a bigger, cross-team investment is overdue rather than a series of one-off fixes.

**Testing:** whether you diagnose a process failure (execution) rather than assuming the analysis itself needs to improve.
